newsitem.title: USA: Dade Cty, Fla., faces cuts or $109.2 mln shortfall.
newsitem.headline: Dade Cty, Fla., faces cuts or $109.2 mln shortfall.

text.p: Florida's Dade County faces a $109.2 million shortfall for fiscal 1998 unless it cuts spending deeply or finds new revenues, county Budget Director Stephen Spratt said Tuesday.

"It's not a deficit because in the end it will be balanced," Spratt told the county commission's Budget, Finance and Public Trust Committee. However, he said, "We do see some very serious cuts coming."
Spratt's projections are for the $2.6 billion operating portion of the county's $4.2 billion budget, for the year beginning Oct 1, 1997.

The county manager will not even submit a proposed budget for that year until May 1. Spratt's report was intended as an early warning to the finance committee that "There will have to be some serious reductions" in that budget.
It reflects what the budget would look like if no changes are made.
Spratt said the county's property tax revenues have decreased more than costs have decreased as wealthy communuties split off from the county government and incorporated as separate cities.

Additionally, an amendment to the state constitution has strictly limited increases in property tax assessments. While Dade's property tax base is growing at about 5 percent a year, only the 2 percent growth that comes from new construction produces added revenues, he said.
When mandated spending, contractual obligations and other fixed costs are figured in, about 75 percent of the county's budget is non-negotiable, he said.
The remaining 25 percent, which includes parks and recreation, public services and internal support, are likley targets for the biggest cuts, he said.
Spratt will begin meeting with county department heads next week to discuss potential budget cuts of up to 10 percent.
He said the present projections are based on the first four months of fiscal 1997, adding, "The numbers may improve as the year progresses."
At this time a year ago, Dade County projected a $75 million shortfall for fiscal 1997, and adjusted its budget accordingly to close the gap.
The projections for an even larger shortfall next year mean the county will have to make even deeper cuts or raise fees to stay in the black in fiscal 1998, he said.
